# Peripartum Cardiomyopathy: An Update on Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management

### Introduction and Epidemiology
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a life-threatening form of heart failure that affects women of childbearing age, characterized by left ventricular (LV) dysfunction (typically a left ventricular ejection fraction [LVEF] < 45%) presenting towards the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery, in the absence of any other identifiable cause of heart failure [1, 2]. Globally, the incidence of PPCM varies widely, ranging from approximately 1 in 100 to 1 in 4,000 live births, with a particularly high prevalence in regions such as South Africa and Haiti, and rising trends in the United States [3, 4]. Key clinical risk factors include advanced maternal age, multiparity, multiple gestations, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (such as preeclampsia), and African ancestry, which is associated with more severe presentations and poorer outcomes [3, 5].

### Pathophysiology
The etiology of PPCM was historically poorly understood, but recent molecular and genetic breakthroughs have illuminated its pathogenesis as a vascular-hormonal mismatch. A pivotal mechanism involves the oxidative-stress-induced cleavage of the hormone prolactin by cathepsin D, generating a 16-kDa prolactin fragment [6]. This fragment is highly anti-angiogenic, pro-inflammatory, and pro-apoptotic, causing endothelial damage and subsequent cardiomyocyte dysfunction [6]. Additionally, late-pregnancy secretion of soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase 1 (sFlt-1) by the placenta further exacerbates angiogenic imbalance, contributing to myocardial injury [7]. 

Genetic studies have revealed a strong hereditary component in PPCM. Approximately 10% to 15% of affected women carry pathogenic gene variants, most commonly truncating mutations in the titin gene (*TTN*), which overlap significantly with those found in dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) [8, 9]. This genetic overlap suggests that PPCM may represent an unmasked pre-existing genetic predisposition exposed by the profound hemodynamic stresses of late pregnancy [9, 10].

### Diagnosis and Clinical Presentation
Patients with PPCM typically present with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, fatigue, peripheral edema, and occasionally cardiogenic shock or thromboembolic events [11]. Because these symptoms mimic physiological late-pregnancy changes, diagnosis is often delayed, leading to worse clinical outcomes [12, 13]. Diagnostic confirmation relies on echocardiography showing an LVEF < 45%, frequently accompanied by left ventricular dilation [10, 14]. Biomarkers like B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) or N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP) are crucial for screening and assessing disease severity, though they lack specificity [15].

### Management and the Role of Bromocriptine
The therapeutic strategy for PPCM requires a multidisciplinary approach, adjusting standard heart failure regimens to ensure maternal and fetal safety. During pregnancy, angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitors (ARNIs), and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are strictly contraindicated due to fetotoxicity [15, 16]. Instead, management relies on beta-blockers, hydralazine, nitrates, and loop diuretics for decongestion [16]. Post-delivery, treatment should be optimized with standard guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT), including ACE inhibitors or ARNIs and MRAs [16, 17].

Based on the pathophysiology of the 16-kDa prolactin fragment, the dopamine agonist bromocriptine has emerged as a disease-specific therapy to block pituitary prolactin release [17, 18]. Randomized clinical trials, including the proof-of-concept pilot study [17] and the subsequent multicenter German BOARD trial [18], have shown that adding bromocriptine to standard GDMT significantly improves LV recovery and clinical outcomes. Because bromocriptine suppresses lactation and increases the risk of thromboembolic events, it must be accompanied by therapeutic anticoagulation [18, 19]. In patients with refractory cardiogenic shock, temporary mechanical circulatory support or levosimendan may be required as a bridge to recovery or transplantation [19, 20].

### Prognosis and Subsequent Pregnancies
The prognosis of PPCM has dramatically improved with contemporary GDMT, with a substantial portion of women achieving partial or complete myocardial recovery (LVEF ≥ 50%) within 6 to 12 months [21, 22]. However, severe LV dysfunction at presentation (LVEF < 30%) and the absence of recovery at 6 months remain strong predictors of long-term morbidity and mortality [23, 24].

For women who have recovered, counseling regarding future pregnancies is critical. Subsequent pregnancies carry a high risk of relapse, even in women with normalized LV function [25, 26]. In those with persistent LV dysfunction (LVEF < 50%), a subsequent pregnancy is associated with high rates of clinical deterioration, heart failure relapse, and maternal mortality, and is therefore strongly discouraged [25, 27]. Careful risk stratification, counseling, and close multidisciplinary monitoring in specialized centers are essential for managing these high-risk patients [28, 29, 30].
